Can I use a siliconflow API key with Claude Code or any other CLI tool?
ChatGPT Plus

No, you cannot use a SiliconFlow API key directly with Claude Code or other CLI tools unless:

  1. The CLI tool explicitly supports SiliconFlow as a backend, or

  2. The SiliconFlow endpoint is fully compatible with the API format expected by the tool (e.g., OpenAI or Anthropic-style endpoints).

Let's break it down:

🔸 SiliconFlow

  • SiliconFlow acts as a proxy or aggregator that provides access to various AI models (like Claude, GPT, etc.) through its own API keys.

  • If you're using a SiliconFlow key, you're typically expected to use their own API endpoint and API format.

🔸 Claude Code (e.g., claude CLI tool)

  • Usually expects Anthropic-compatible API keys and endpoints.

  • If you try to use a SiliconFlow key directly in a CLI tool expecting Anthropic’s native API, it will not work unless SiliconFlow mimics the full Anthropic API structure.

✅ What can work

If you're using a CLI like llm (from llm.ai) or openllm that allows:

  • Custom base URLs

  • Custom headers (e.g., Authorization: Bearer <key>)

Then you might be able to configure it to use SiliconFlow’s API if:

  • The tool supports the request format SiliconFlow expects.

  • SiliconFlow provides the model you want (e.g., Claude, GPT-4, etc.).

🔧 Example (only if supported):

If SiliconFlow says to call:

bash
POST https://api.siliconflow.com/v1/completions
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_KEY

And the CLI tool lets you customize the endpoint, then you might try:

bash
llm --api-url https://api.siliconflow.com/v1 --api-key YOUR_KEY

But that only works if SiliconFlow’s API format matches what the tool expects (e.g., OpenAI-compatible for completions/chat).

✅ What to do

  1. Check if the CLI tool supports SiliconFlow natively.

  2. If not, check if the CLI lets you set custom endpoints and headers.

  3. Look up the API format SiliconFlow uses (OpenAI-style? Anthropic-style?).

  4. Optionally: Use a wrapper script or middleware if formats don’t match.

Yes, you can use your SiliconFlow API key with a CLI tool — but only if that CLI supports custom endpoints compatible with the OpenAI API, because SiliconFlow provides an OpenAI‑compatible REST interface. Here's how it works:

✅ How CLI Support Works

According to the SiliconFlow quickstart documentation:

  • SiliconFlow’s large‑model APIs can be invoked using the OpenAI Python library.

  • You specify a custom base URL:

    python
    from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(api_key="YOUR_SF_KEY",
                base_url="https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1")
...

    GitHub+3docs.siliconflow.cn+3YouTube+3GitHub+3cnblogs.com+3siliconflow.cn+3

  • They support common OpenAI-style params, like model, messages, stream, etc. docs.siliconflow.cn

This means any CLI tool built to be OpenAI-compatible—including those based on openai or with similar flags—can work with SiliconFlow by redirecting calls.

🔧 Practical Steps for CLI Tools

1. openai-cli (OpenAI’s official tool)

You can set environment variables to redirect it:

bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="YOUR_SF_KEY"
export OPENAI_API_BASE="https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1"
openai chat completions create --model "Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct" --messages '[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]'

2. Custom CLIs / scripts using OpenAI SDKs

Replace the default endpoint in code:

bash
openai api chat.completions.create \
  --api-key "$SF_KEY" \
  --base https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1 \
  --model "DeepSeek-R1" \
  --messages '[{"role":"user","content":"Hi!"}]'

3. Other CLIs (llama.cpp-style, openllm, etc.)

Check if they support:

  • --base-url or --api-url

  • Your SF API key as --api-key

  • And use OpenAI-like request format

If yes → ✅ likely good to go.

✅ Summary

  • Works: Any CLI with adjustable OpenAI endpoint parameters, since SiliconFlow is OpenAI-compatible Zhihu.

  • Won’t work: Tools hard-coded for Anthropic/Claude-style APIs or proprietary formats — unless they add custom endpoint support.

🚀 What You Should Do Next

  1. Choose the CLI tool you want to use (e.g., openai-cli, openai-sdk-based script, or other community tool).

  2. Verify it lets you override API_BASE, --api-url, or similar.

  3. Point it to https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1 and use your SF API key.

  4. Test by calling a simple model (e.g., Qwen, DeepSeek).

Perfect! Here's how to configure the official OpenAI CLI to work with SiliconFlow.

✅ Step-by-Step Setup: openai CLI with SiliconFlow

🧰 Prerequisites

You need:

  • The official OpenAI CLI installed (pip install openai)

  • A SiliconFlow API key

  • A terminal

🔧 1. Set the Environment Variables

Run this in your terminal, replacing YOUR_API_KEY with your SiliconFlow API key:

bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY"
export OPENAI_API_BASE="https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1"

You can add these lines to your ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or ~/.profile to persist them.

🧪 2. Test a Simple Chat Completion

SiliconFlow supports OpenAI-compatible models like Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V2, etc.

Try this:

bash
openai chat completions create \
  --model "Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct" \
  --messages '[{"role":"user","content":"Hola, ¿quién eres?"}]'

You should receive a response from the model. If not, the error will help debug issues (e.g., invalid model name or expired key).

📄 3. List Available Models (Optional)

Try this to see what models SiliconFlow offers:

bash
openai models.list

If this doesn’t work, it’s because SiliconFlow doesn’t implement the /models route. In that case, use their docs to find available model names.

Some known working ones (from the docs):

  • "Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct"

  • "DeepSeek-V2", "DeepSeek-R1"

  • "Yi-1.5-9B-Chat", "Baichuan2-53B-Chat"

✅ You're All Set

You can now use the openai CLI just like with OpenAI, but with SiliconFlow as the backend.

❌ The CLI is still calling OpenAI’s servers, not SiliconFlow’s, even though you provided your SiliconFlow key.

That’s because the openai api ... command ignores the OPENAI_API_BASE environment variable in many versions of the CLI, unless it's patched or explicitly supported — and it strictly expects OpenAI keys that start with sk-.

✅ Solution: Use Python Script or curl Instead

Since the CLI is forcing OpenAI’s platform, let’s switch to a fully controllable method.

🔧 Option A: Python Script (most reliable)

  1. Install the latest SDK:

bash
pip install --upgrade openai

  1. Create sf_chat.py:

python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_SILICONFLOW_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Hola, ¿quién eres?"}
    ]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

  1. Run:

bash
python sf_chat.py

🌀 Option B: Raw curl request

bash
curl https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SILICONFLOW_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hola, ¿quién eres?"}]
  }'

✅ Summary

  • The official OpenAI CLI isn’t compatible because it enforces OpenAI’s platform and key format.

  • Use Python (openai.OpenAI(...)) or curl to work directly with SiliconFlow.

  • ✅ SiliconFlow is OpenAI-compatible, but only when you control the HTTP layer or use SDKs that support base_url.

✅ Step-by-Step: Use llm with SiliconFlow

bash
pip install llm

2. Add a SiliconFlow model

You only need to do this once:

bash
llm add-remote siliconflow \
  --base-url https://api.siliconflow.cn/v1 \
  --api-key sk-...your-sf-key... \
  --models Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct \
  --alias sf-qwen

You can repeat this for other models like DeepSeek-V2, Baichuan2-53B-Chat, etc.

3. Use it!

bash
llm -m sf-qwen "¿Cuál es la capital de Francia?"

This sends the prompt to SiliconFlow through the llm CLI.

🧪 Bonus: Show Model Output with Streaming

bash
llm -m sf-qwen --stream "Escribe un haiku sobre los gatos y el silencio"

🧩 You Can Also:

Thanks — that’s the key clue. The messages:

❌ "Plan not supported"
❌ "Agent not supported"

mean that your selected model from SiliconFlow (e.g. Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) does not support Dev Mode features like tools, agents, or plan generation — at least as Continue understands them.

⚠️ Why This Happens

Continue.dev relies on specific model capabilities for Dev Mode (code-aware planning, tool invocation, diff-aware responses).

Models like GPT-4, Claude 3, or Gemini 1.5 have:

  • Advanced reasoning

  • Code structure understanding

  • Support for Continue’s tool API

But SiliconFlow serves Open-source models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Yi…), which:

  • Do not support planning/agent interfaces by default

  • Are often chat-only, not optimized for structured editing tools

🧭 Your Options

✅ Option 1: Use Chat Mode + Manual Edits

You can still use the chat mode with Qwen or DeepSeek to ask:

“Can you rewrite this function to be async?”
“Suggest improvements to this block of code”

But you’ll have to manually apply those suggestions. No tools, no diffs.

✅ Option 2: Switch to a Fully Supported Model (if available)

If you can use OpenAI GPT-4 or Anthropic Claude 3 via their official keys (or a proxy that supports tools/agents), you’ll get:

✅ Plan generation
✅ File system tools
✅ Diff previews
✅ Full Gemini/Claude Code-like behavior

❌ No Known SiliconFlow Models Support Dev Mode

As of now, SiliconFlow does not offer Claude 3, GPT-4, or Gemini. Their models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Yi) are chat-only, so Dev Mode is disabled.

✅ Workaround: Fake Dev Mode via Prompt Engineering

You can still try this trick:

  1. Open a file

  2. Select the code

  3. In chat, ask:

    “Refactor the selected function and show me a unified diff.”

Some models (like DeepSeek or Yi) can generate diffs in text format.

You then manually apply the diff.
